slides.say: Now volume. The volume is what's inside the solid, how much it can hold.

slides: Think of a bottle of water. The label says five hundred milliliters. That's the volume of the water.

slides.say: A cubic centimeter is a tiny cube, one centimeter by one centimeter by one centimeter.
at: A cubic centimeter is a tiny cube

slides.say: And one milliliter is exactly one cubic centimeter. So the bottle holds five hundred cubic centimeters.
Now look at a rectangle, two by three. It has an area, but no volume. It's flat.
Let's put another rectangle on top of it, and another, and another. Each one alone is flat. But together they make a box, and the box takes up space.
So the volume of the box is the area of its base, times its height. We take the base area again and again, as many times as the height.
at: So the volume of the box

slides.say: Our box is two by three, with height four. The base area is two times three, six. And six times four is twenty-four. So for a box, it's length times width times height.
A cube with edge five is five times five times five, one hundred twenty-five. That's five to the power of three.
The cylinder works the same way. Its base is a circle, pi r squared, and we multiply it by the height. With radius three and height five, the base is nine pi, and nine pi times five is forty-five pi.
And the same for any prism. If the base of a triangular prism has area twelve and its height is ten, its volume is twelve times ten, one hundred twenty.
On the exam we also have pointed solids. They're not prisms.
A cone has a circle at the bottom, and at the top only a point, like a party hat.
Put a cylinder around it, with the same base and the same height. The cone's volume is one third of that cylinder.
at: The cone's volume is one third

slides.say: Our cylinder had radius three and height five, and its volume was forty-five pi. So a cone with the same base and height is forty-five pi divided by three, fifteen pi.
A pyramid has a polygon at the bottom, a triangle, a square, a hexagon, it doesn't matter. And at the top, one point.
Its volume is the base area, times the height, divided by three.
at: Its volume is the base area

slides.say: Let's take a pyramid with a square base, six by six, and height five. The base area is six times six, thirty-six.
Thirty-six times five is one hundred eighty. Divided by three, that's sixty.
And one hundred eighty is the box around the pyramid, six by six by five. So the pyramid is one third of that box.

slides: So a pointed solid is always one third of the straight solid with the same base and the same height.

slides.say: One more thing. The height goes straight down, from the point to the middle of the base. It is not this slanted edge, which is longer.
at: It is not this slanted edge

slides.say: Good news. At the start of every quantitative section, there's a formula page.
It has the volume and the surface area of a box and of a cube. It has the cylinder's lateral area, total area and volume. And it has the volume of a cone and of a pyramid.
It doesn't have the general rules we learned for any prism. And it doesn't have the ideas of the next lessons. Those you need to know yourself.
at: It doesn't have the general rules

slides.say: So let's sum up. The lateral area is everything that wraps around. It's the perimeter of the base, times the height.
The total surface area is the lateral area plus the two bases.
The volume is everything inside. It's the base area, times the height.
And a pointed solid, a cone or any pyramid, has the same volume divided by three. Always.

slides: Take a moment to memorize these, and I'll see you in the next video.
